reason: The sources provide enough factual claims about the 2025 live discovery of a juvenile colossal squid to support a short.
story: For a century after its scientific description in 1925, the colossal squid was a ghost. Known mostly from dead specimens, beaks, and scars on sperm whales, the heaviest invertebrate on Earth had never been filmed alive in its natural habitat. That changed on March 9, 2025. During an expedition near the South Sandwich Islands in the South Atlantic, an international team using the Schmidt Ocean Institute's remotely operated vehicle SuBastian captured the first confirmed live footage of the species. Instead of a tentacle-thrashing monster, the camera revealed a translucent juvenile, measuring about 12 inches long, drifting at a depth of 600 meters. The sighting bridged a century-long gap in marine biology, giving scientists their first real look at the living animal in the deep sea.
angle: The colossal squid is the heaviest invertebrate on Earth, yet for 100 years science had never seen one alive until a baby was finally filmed in 2025.

claims.claim: The colossal squid was first filmed alive in its natural habitat on March 9, 2025.
The live footage captured a juvenile colossal squid measuring about 30 centimeters or 12 inches long.
The juvenile colossal squid was filmed at a depth of 600 meters or nearly 2,000 feet.
The sighting took place during an expedition near the South Sandwich Islands in the South Atlantic Ocean.
The footage was recorded by the Schmidt Ocean Institute's remotely operated vehicle ROV SuBastian.
The colossal squid species was formally described in 1925 by Guy Coburn Robson.
The species was originally discovered from two arm crowns found in the stomach of a sperm whale.
The colossal squid is the heaviest known invertebrate, reaching weights of at least 495 to 500 kilograms or 1,100 pounds.
Colossal squid possess hooks on their arms and tentacles.
For 100 years, scientists encountered colossal squids mainly as prey remains in whale and seabird stomachs and as predators of harvested toothfish.
Adult colossal squid are estimated to reach lengths of up to 7 meters or 23 feet.
The expedition that captured the footage was a collaboration involving the Ocean Census, the Schmidt Ocean Institute, and other partners.

disputed: Maximum length estimates vary between sources, with some citing total lengths up to 14 meters when measuring stretched tentacles on dead specimens while body length estimates generally cite up to 7 meters. Scripts should attribute maximum lengths to dead specimen measurements.
